Then one mysterious Monday, you receive a letter from your family lawyer informing you that a long-lost relative has bequeathed you a factory. You decide to risk it all, quit your day job, and follow your dream to become the greatest board game manufacturer the world has ever seen! You'll have to hire staff, build an assembly line, invest in additional structures to your factory, gain and fulfill contracts, and market your line of board games to the world. In The Game Makers, players are board game manufacturers racing to build the greatest collection of classic modern board games. Build over 300 real-world games from over 100 real-world publishers. You can build Wingspan, Brass: Birmingham, On Mars, Terraforming Mars, Ark Nova, and many more! The central warehouse rondel which dominates the center of the gaming table has players simultaneously choosing which game components to manufacture in a given turn and how to use them. The Game Makers features not only multi-use cards but also other multi-use components. Will you use these components to fulfill a coveted contract or upgrade your factory? Gain the necessary requirements to manufacture a game, and then add it to your display case of legendary games! Will you manufacture your favorite board game? Or will you manufacture the game you hate for more points? Score points from the games that you built and how well you marketed them. The Game Makers is a love letter to the board gaming hobby. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 1.1 How does the game work? 1.2 The Warehouse Wheel 2 Components 2.1 Contracts/Cards 2.2 Workers/Wood 2.3 Enhancements 2.4 Marketing/Dice 2.5 Machinery/Punchboard (blue octagons) 2.6 Buildings/Plastic 2.7 Trees 3 End Game 3.1 Scoring Overview The Game Makers is a worker-placement game where each player takes turns gathering components to build the world's greatest games. Along the way, unneeded components can be repurposed to form workers, structures, and other upgrades to increase your factory's efficiency. Fill your display case and become the greatest game maker ever. How does the game work? There is no turn order. Each player takes their turn simultaneously, moving their forklifts from the "ready" position to a part of the warehouse. A new turn cannot begin until all forklifts are out of the "ready" position. When all players have finished, the warehouse wheel turns and moves to the next wedge, changing which components are available. You can move your forklifts to any available space, even a space that has your own or another player's forklifts on it. The Warehouse Wheel The warehouse wheel is how you control your workers and gain components to build games. When your forklift(s) are in the "ready" zone, you move them to a space to gain that component. After moving, the forklift cannot be moved again until it's returned to the "ready" position. Each component's "quality" (level 3, 2, or 1) is related to its distance from the "ready" position. A level 3 component will be the furthest away, thus taking the most time to get your forklift back to ready after retrieving it. Components When you take a resource, you must decide whether to use it as a component or a company asset. Each component serves two purposes. One is as a game part ( component ). The other is used for upgrading your factory ( company asset ) and is unique to each type of resource. Once you decide, you cannot switch it back. [Rating: 1/10] Over-produced game that is gimmicky to sell product instead of a decent game. Typical crowdfunding trap. Stay away from such projects and buy stuff that is leaner and cleaner and most importantly playtested. Don’t listen to influencers they only hype stuff up as they receieve free products or demo copies "for content" which is sketch as heck. This game is a perfect example of product before game aka short-term sales are more important than quality and longevity.

[Rating: 2/10] Sadly just unimaginative, generic euro slob. Looks nice, though. No interations between players. Kickstarter FOMO (exclusives). Agressive marketing via Nostalgia Marketing and "Loveletter to gaming" (no guys, its really just business) Green-washing a much plastic game via "tree planting" and Pandas "enviromental commitment" (do we still believe this despite the evidences?) 95% marketing, 5% game. played on BGA.

[Rating: 2/10] The designers clearly put a lot of thought into the game's depth and strategic complexity, and experienced hobby gamers will find a lot to explore. That said, this is not a game for casual board gamers. The rules and mechanics have a steep learning curve, and many systems aren't especially intuitive for new players. If you're looking for an easy game to teach or play with beginners, this probably isn't the best choice.

[Rating: 3/10] I feel like I want to like this, but turns feel like a chore, and it seems like there's just too much going on.

[Rating: 3/10] Not for me. One of (if not) the most multiplayer solitare game I have ever played. Extremely overproduced with a ton of plastic for a game that even has big environmental gameplay element of "Go Green".  I understand that the game draws a lot of attention because it has a bunch of cards with cover art from known games, good production and simultaneous turns though.

[Rating: 3/10] Insanely overpriced, ugly artwork, simple loop of gathering resources and fulfilling orders but convoluted ruleset, confusing icons and hodgepodge of many mechanics (worker placement, tile laying, set collections....) that was done better in other games

[Rating: 3/10] Decent overproduced game, but it feels a bit indulgent when playing it which is nice.

[Rating: 4/10] This game has some nice mechanics, but it is a shame that it is completely solitaire.

[Rating: 4/10] Almost zero interaction, the only existing one is triggering the end game that makes others hurry as well. What is this game?!?

[Rating: 4/10] It was neat and the theme was cool but there was way too little interaction for my taste. Note that I usually feel that way about this type of game, but this game made me feel like it was effort to care what anyone else was doing. If you don't care about that then this might be a great game for you.

[Rating: 5/10] This is like Castle Combo and Race for the Galaxy combined into a medium weight game. Deceptively easy to play, but the more I tried to formulate a strategy, the more it hurt my head. I felt overwhelmed for a medium complexity game that throws so many options at every turn.

[Rating: 5/10] I wanted to love this. I might yet! But it's solitary (little interaction beyond racing to end the game -- which does matter a lot!) and the games are not as different from one another as I would have hoped. Gamers... and not just any gamers, but the sort who would play a game like this... might not all fancy the idea of every set collection game being kind of the same. Or maybe they will! I love the idea enough to give it another try, I just also love the idea enough to have come in with big expectations.  [1 play, on BGA]

[Rating: 5/10] This game bills itself as a love letter to the hobby, but it's really more of a love letter to the industry, and more specifically the manufacturing segment of the industry, and more specifically the manufacturing segment of the industry that is located in China.  My understanding is that the designer is an employee of a Chinese manufacturer, and "write what you know", ok, fair enough.    But for me, the "love letter to the hobby" fell flat.  The model is that a game is, fundamentally, two things:  the set of components that go in the box, and a bonus/reward, often for some spatial arrangement
